scenes.title: Call Delta vs. Put Delta Formulas & Dividend Adjustments

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Call Delta: Delta_call = N(d1) for non-dividend stocks, adjusting to e^(-q*T)*N(d1) when continuous dividend yield q is present ([fact-03]).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Compare Put Delta: Delta_put = N(d1) - 1, representing negative price sensitivity for short put positions ([fact-03]).

summarySteps: 1. Naive Hedging Pitfalls ([fact-01]): Naked writing exposes institutions to catastrophic losses, while covered positions suffer severe equity drawdowns during market crashes.
2. Stop-Loss Whipsaws ([fact-02]): Stop-loss strategies accumulate severe transaction costs and cash leakage due to frequent price oscillations around strike K.
3. Option Delta Formulas ([fact-03]): Delta measures price sensitivity, equal to N(d1) for calls and N(d1) - 1 for puts.
4. Delta Neutrality Sizing ([fact-04]): Writing Q options requires purchasing Q * Delta underlying shares to neutralize linear price risk.
5. Dynamic Rebalancing ([fact-05]): As stock prices and time shift, delta changes continuously, requiring periodic share purchases or sales to maintain neutrality.
6. Real-World Friction ([fact-06]): Institutions use tolerance bands (+/- 0.05) or fixed calendar intervals to balance Gamma slippage against transaction commissions.

7. Gamma Risk and Taylor Series ([fact-08], [fact-09]): Delta hedging is linear; large discrete price jumps expose portfolios to non-linear Gamma curvature governed by second-order Taylor approximations.
8. Hedging Cost Equivalency ([fact-10]): The expected present value of cumulative dynamic hedging costs exactly equals the upfront option premium received (no free alpha).
bottomTakeaway: Dynamic delta hedging transforms option directional exposure into rebalancing and transaction friction, requiring continuous Greek management and Gamma risk control ([fact-04], [fact-07], [fact-09], [fact-10]).
